STATEMENT BY DEPUTY MINISTER OF FINANCE RESPECTING EFFECTIVENESS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask the unanimous consent of the House under Standing Order 43 to move a motion on a matter of urgent and
pressing necessity.
This matter concerns the confidence of the government in the Economic Council of Canada, whether the Deputy Minister of Finance, Mr. Simon Reisman, was authorized by his minister, who was then present, to state yesterday before the Senate Committee on National Finance that "after seven years the Economic Council of Canada has run out of steam, is repeating itself and should be revitalized," and whether the government shares these views that its chief economic advisers are out of tune with the times and must be replaced. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave):
That the testimony of the Deputy Minister of Finance before the Senate Committee on National Finance relative to the Economic Council of Canada, its views and operations, and any related question be referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for examination and report, and that the Minister of Finance and his Deputy Minister, Mr. Simon Reisman, be invited to appear to testify on the said matters.

speechtext: Question No. 352

subtopic: DUPLICATION OF INFORMATION COLLECTED BY DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR AND DBS
speechtext:
1.	What action has been taken, or what measures are contemplated, by the Minister of Labour to eliminate the duplication caused by his Department continuing to collect, on a voluntary basis, the same kind of information from unions that must he included in the annual returns filed by unions with the Dominion Statistician pursuant to Section 9(a) of the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act?
2.	Has the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce sanctioned, or concurred in, any changes or amendments to the reporting requirements of Part II of the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act and, if so, what are these changes or amendments?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Jerome (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DUPLICATION OF INFORMATION COLLECTED BY DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR AND DBS
speechtext:
I am informed by the Department of Labour and Statistics Canada (Dominion Bureau of Statistics) as follows: 1. Early in 1970, interdepartmental arrangements were developed aimed at eliminating the duplication caused by the concurrent operation of the Department of Labour's annual survey of labour organizations and the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act. Under these arrangements, information submitted by unions to the Department of Labour in fulfilment of the January 1, 1971 survey requirements will be made available to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics to satisfy the major portion of the requirements of Section 9(a) of the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act. For this reason, certain additional items of information will be requested of unions by the Department of Labour in the January 1971 survey.
2.	At the request of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, arrangements were developed with the Department of Labour early in 1970 whereby information submitted to the Canada Department of Labour in fulfilment of that department's January 1, 1971 survey requirements would be used to satisfy the major portion of the 1970 reporting requirements of Section 9(a) of the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act. For this reason, the Department of Labour's survey coverage for January 1, 1971 was extended to include certain additional items of information. This arrangement does not reduce the legislative requirements of the Corporations and

June 30, 1971
Questions
Labour Unions Returns Act. Information not available through the Canada Department of Labour survey will be obtained directly by Statistics Canada (Dominion Bureau of Statistics).
The following reporting requirements are affected by this arrangement: (a) The major portion of Section A is filed indirectly with the Dominion Statistician, (b) The reference date for the reporting is January 1, 1971. This will affect only unions with fiscal year-end other than December 31, 1970. (c) The signature of the union official submitting the report to the Canada Department of Labour survey is accepted, for that report, in lieu of the verifications by two executive board members.

subtopic: MARGOULIS-CHOUBLADZE VACCINE
MARGOULIS-CHOUBLADZE VACCINE
speechtext:
1.	Are the researchers of the Department of National Health and Welfare or any other department aware of the existence of a Russian vaccination bearing the name Margoulis-Choubladze for the treatment of multiple sclerosis and, if so, has the government authorized research with respect to this vaccination?
2.	Did the Russian laboratory V/O Medexport submit a registration application for this medicine to Canada either directly or through the Russian Embassy in Ottawa and, if not, is the government willing to accept such an application?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: MARGOULIS-CHOUBLADZE VACCINE
speechtext:
1. The Margoulis-Choubladze vaccine has been known to officers of the Food and Drug Directorate for
Questions
many years. The earliest published reference to this vaccine appeared in 1946, and in 1957 it was studied extensively in both Britain and the United States. According to information in the medical literature, the vaccine is prepared from the brains of rats or mice infected with a virus which cause acute encephalitis (inflammation of the brain) in man. Since the manufacturer of the Margoulis-Choubladze vaccine has not provided the Food and Drug Directorate with data in accordance with the Food and Drugs Act and Regulations, the importation of this vaccine into Canada and its distribution or sale for administration to humans would be in violation of the law.
2.	In the Spring of 1970 an official of the Embassy of the U.S.S.R. telephoned a senior officer of the Food and Drug Directorate and requested information concerning the Canadian regulations governing the importation and sale of this vaccine in Canada. It was explained to him that the manufacturer would be required to submit complete information to substantiate its safety and effectiveness in the treatment of multiple sclerosis and that until such information is received and found to be satisfactory, the importation of this vaccine into Canada would not be permitted. The Soviet official stated that he had in his possession some literature from the Russian company V/O Medexport pertaining to this vaccine. He asked if the Food and Drug Directorate would be willing to review this material and tell him what additional data would be required in a formal submission. Officers of the Food and Drug Directorate readily agreed to his proposal. Subsequently, documents describing the clinical results obtained with the vaccine were received from the Embassy of the U.S.S.R. and were reviewed. Detailed comments were then transmitted to the Embassy of the U.S.S.R. Advice was given as to the type and extent of additional data which the Directorate would require for inclusion in a formal submission as with any other drug proposed for sale in Canada. However, to date no such submission has been received. If and when such a submission is received, it will be promptly reviewed by officers of the Food and Drug Directorate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FLORENCE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
1. The United Nations lists 63 countries for which the "Florence Agreement" on the Importation of Educational, Scientific and Cultural Materials has entered into force.
2. Canada is not a signatory of the "Florence Agreement". Canada has not signed the Agreement because it has not been considered to be in Canada's interest to abandon the limited protection afforded domestic producers against imports of certain educational, scientific and cultural materials as long as important trading partners maintained barriers against Canadian exports of these materials. Canada does impose small duty on such imports but other countries, even where no tariffs are maintained, continue to limit imports from Canada of these materials by the use of stringent non tariff barriers. In any event the question of Canada's accession is under continuous review in the light of changing conditions in trade and in the light of the report submitted on March 23, 1971, by the Economic Council, based on its intensive study of aspects of cultural property.

subtopic: POVERTY LEVEL
POVERTY LEVEL
speechtext: What does the Department of National Health and Welfare consider to be the acceptable "poverty level" of income for a single person and for a married couple with one wage earner?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: POVERTY LEVEL
speechtext: The Department of National Health and Welfare does not use the concept of an acceptable "poverty level" of income. Although the Economic Council of Canada and other agencies have used the term in order to measure the extent of poverty in Canada, the levels of income which they describe as poverty level are necessarily based on opinion and judgment as to what constitutes an acceptable level of income for a given situation. The Department attempts to provide a basic level of income to low income aged persons in Canada. Thus in 1971, it has provided a minimum monthly income of $135 for a single person and $255 for a married couple. This amounts to $1,620 and $3,060 a year respectively. Through the Old Age Security Act as revised, the government has provided that no person over the age of 65 who meets the residence requirements will have less than these amounts to live on.

subtopic: PROPOSED TAPS TANKER ROUTE-APPROVAL INDICATED BY UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF THE INTERIOR-EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN OPPOSITION
PROPOSED TAPS TANKER ROUTE-APPROVAL INDICATED BY UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF THE INTERIOR-EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN OPPOSITION
speechtext: My question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the statement by the United States Secretary of the Interior yesterday that the TAPS route will be approved, were Canadian officials advised of this statement and, if so, did they express the strong opposition of the Parliament of Canada to the approval of this route?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED TAPS TANKER ROUTE-APPROVAL INDICATED BY UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF THE INTERIOR-EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN OPPOSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a number of statements have been made that the TAPS line will be approved, but until the United States government does give its approval, of course, these are all just expressions of opinion. The Canadian government has made it very clear that its concern is about tankers entering the narrow waters of the Strait of Juan de Fuca and the Strait of Georgia. It is on this point that we are making our representations to the United States.

subtopic: PROPOSED TAPS TANKER ROUTE-APPROVAL INDICATED BY UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF THE INTERIOR-EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN OPPOSITION
speechtext:
In view of the fact that the use of these waters is of prime concern, as the minister has said, has the United States government assured Canada that the use of these waters, particularly by tankers, will be reconsidered and that our view on this matter will receive serious consideration?
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED TAPS TANKER ROUTE-APPROVAL INDICATED BY UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF THE INTERIOR-EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN OPPOSITION
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, both when I saw Secretary Rogers and again yesterday when an official of the Canadian government met with the State Department. The United States government has made it clear that it is aware of the dangers and they want to talk to us about the means of either minimizing or eliminating the dangers.

subtopic: PROPOSED TAPS TANKER ROUTE-APPROVAL INDICATED BY UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF THE INTERIOR-EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN OPPOSITION
speechtext: As the Secretary of the Interior said yesterday that this decision will be made within 75 days, has the Canadian government made it clear to the United States government that the present state of research in this whole matter does not warrant a final decision being made in that short a space of time?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED TAPS TANKER ROUTE-APPROVAL INDICATED BY UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF THE INTERIOR-EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN OPPOSITION
speechtext: That has been our contention all along, Mr. Speaker. That is why we have made our representations and why various Members of Parliament, particularly on this side, who represent constituencies in British Columbia have been emphasizing this point in their private representations and in their efforts to arouse public opinion in both Canada and the United States against the dangers that lie in the movement of tankers through these narrow waters. We do not believe there has been sufficient attention paid to the dangers.

subtopic: PROPOSED TAPS TANKER ROUTE-APPROVAL INDICATED BY UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF THE INTERIOR-EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN OPPOSITION
speechtext: supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the statement by Secretary of the Interior Morton that it is not a matter of whether the TAPS program will be put into effect but merely when, I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs if he has received any word out of the discussions he said took place yesterday in Washington and if the Canadian representatives at that meeting received any assurance or encouragement that these tankers will not be routed through the Strait of Juan de Fuca or the Strait of Georgia?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED TAPS TANKER ROUTE-APPROVAL INDICATED BY UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF THE INTERIOR-EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN OPPOSITION
speechtext: When our officials met with the State Department officials yesterday, we again emphasized the points I have been making here in the House, that I made to Secretary Rogers and that our officials made previously that no massive movement of oil should take place in the inner waters of British Columbia and the State of Washington. The United States officials have said that they are very much aware of the dangers involved and are having further discussions about this to see whether the route can be altered or, if it is not altered, what can be done to minimize the dangers.

subtopic: PROPOSED TAPS TANKER ROUTE-APPROVAL INDICATED BY UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF THE INTERIOR-EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN OPPOSITION
speechtext: In view of the fact that time seems to be running out, that a definitive decision is about to be taken by the United States and that the discussions to date have been mainly at an official level, will the minister or the Prime Minister undertake to have direct contacts with their counterparts in the United States to prevent what could be a very serious tragedy on the Pacific coast?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED TAPS TANKER ROUTE-APPROVAL INDICATED BY UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF THE INTERIOR-EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN OPPOSITION
speechtext:
I cannot accept that statement as a statement of facts. I have had several conversations with the Secretary of State of the United States on this question.

speechtext:

subtopic: ALLEGED SHIPMENT OF CANADIAN ARMS TO PAKISTAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the procedure in granting export permits is that sometimes permits are given in advance at the time an application is made for shipment at a later date, but always subject to suspension or cancellation of the permits if in the meantime government policy has had to be changed, as it had to be with respect to the particular case involving Pakistan. subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night, I was saying that the economy was on an uneven keel and that there are solutions to restore balance. I also said that the unbalance is caused by financiers who are now taking advantage of the situation. I also stated that banks were creating money and devising means of payment out of nothing, except for small entries in their books and through cheques which they draw on their own funds, thus allowing themselves to negotiate purchases with drafts that do not have much value.
Treasury bills and Canada savings bonds as well as all taxes and surtaxes that we pay are used increasingly to pay the debt unknown to Canadians through financial means that reinforce the discretionary power of banks on the lives of individuals and governments. Therefore, the
June 30, 1971

government has become a mere valet deprived of all sovereignty over the issuance of money and credit.
Whatever government is in power, Canada will always be at the mercy of atrocious finance. This will last until the government regains control over money and credit for natural resources development and financing of public undertakings which would require new credit based on the same values, except that there would be no interest on repayment. This would be done at depreciation cost, at the rate of 5 per cent per year, and all debts should be amortized in 20 years.
Those who tolerate the way the present financial system works are responsible for the present economic chaos. One terrible day, the people will ask for an accounting.
As Canadians develop the country, high finance takes possession of it. Its high priests bear the responsibility for leaving the people in ignorance; it is the just society for the financiers and their friends.
The insecurity, the troubles, and the loss of confidence being felt are due to this absolute control over our lives and our institutions.
The yoke of heartless finance, Mr. Speaker, holds us and sinks us deeper into stagnation. We may try, by all sorts of means, to improve our lot, to find new solutions and methods that would be in accordance with scientific and technological progress, all is useless, because finance exploits us and takes our money as soon as we earn it.
As we borrow, amounts to the credit of Canadians are passed to the credit of financial institutions, through mere bookkeeping entries and the big capitalists become the owners of everything we do or build. They are the masters of our entire economy.
We pay taxes to reimburse those same institutions and over $2 billion in interest this year. They will be paid more interest next year and it will go on year after year, because taxes will again be increased.
We could, Mr. Speaker, grant discounts on prices, which would lower the cost of living. We would settle the problem or if we prefer, we would make up the difference through a dividend. Thus 22 million Canadians would have 22 million times as much purchasing power.
We lack purchasing power because there is not enough money in circulation, and the money does not circulate long enough, for it is withdrawn much too soon by the financial system. Furthermore, the reimbursement of money plus interest causes the economy to be unsteady. It thus becomes practically impossible to develop the economy and to create any economic stability which would benefit the population. That diabolical system throws the economy off balance as solutions are being investigated.
Mr. Speaker, what we need to solve this problem is the guaranteed income directly payable from 1971 surpluses.
During 1971, our production was $90 billion; consumption was $54 billion and capitalization $36 billion, includ-
The Budget-Mr. Lang
ing $30 billion capitalized by big corporations as against $6 billion only by individuals.
That is one of the only ways of restoring economic balance and distributing the wealth to Canadian people almost without levying taxes since there would be no more debts. Taxes would be levied only to pay government administration, which would probably not exceed 1 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, until we take the necessary means to put the economy on an even keel through a financial system that would be sounder, more adequate, more in accordance with reality, we shall experience difficulties. Economists will keep on making investigations of all kinds, they will try to find all sorts of means, will bring up numerous programs and new departments will be created in order to serve the people and stabilize our economy. But the more we will play that game, the more our economy will be out of kilter. As time goes on, we sink deeper, the economic situation is getting worse and the people enjoy fewer services and are less satisfied.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otlo E. Lang (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget this year culminated a long period of very intensive discussion in Canada about our taxation system. It included, of course, the announcement of immediate tax changes and of changes for a number of years to come. In the course of making these changes, it was possible to examine the way in which the existing tax load is borne by different segments of our community and to look again at what should be included as income for taxation purposes when determining who should pay and how much.
The most significant addition on the side of taxes, where taxes had not been collected before, was the introduction of a capital gains tax in Canada for the first time. With this introduction we were, of course, simply joining many other areas of the world where this particular form of improvement in position had been subject to tax for some years. The inclusion of capital gains as income for taxation purposes at one half the rate of other accretions does, in fact, introduce into the treasury eventually a very significant amount of money. The half rate is justifiable in terms of the significant possibility that a portion of any apparent gain is in reality an adjustment in terms of the value of the dollars being obtained in the sale of a product. Including half, therefore, allows for a partial offset against the effect of inflation in raising the value of goods which it would be unfair to tax in full. The introduction of additional income in this manner, and in some other ways, within the budget meant that it was possible to raise the amount of money required with a reduction in tax in some very important areas.
The most fundamental improvements really attach to the increase in personal exemptions which will be occur-ing with the commencement of 1972. The increase in exemption to $1,500 for a single taxpayer and to $2,850 for a married taxpayer means that a much greater portion of the money earned by low income groups, working

June 30, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Lang
people whose incomes are not high, is left in their hands. More important, Canadians are satisfied that we must do many things to assist those who have levels of income lower than some desirable target in order that they may have the means to a decent livelihood. What could be more sensible, then, than to leave in the hands of those who are working, but whose income levels have not approached this target, more of their income; what could be more sensible than to shift the tax burden, the payment of taxes in whole, from those at very low levels of earning power and in significant degree from those at relatively low levels of earning power, to others in our community?
This shifting of our tax burden assists the lower income groups wherever they may be. It assists the worker in the city, it assists the man on minimum wage, it assists the farmer in difficult circumstances and it assists all of these in recognition of their own efforts to attempt to earn an income, to attempt on their own to supply themselves and their families with what they need. It recognizes that in these circumstances the general services provided in Canada through the government, and through the taxpayers generally for all, should be paid for by those who have more and who therefore can better afford to support the services which we all want. This kind of change does have a significant impact in the farming communities of Canada. These are areas where for many years a good number of people, working hard at producing a livelihood for themselves and producing great value for Canada, have had incomes in the lower levels. The higher exemptions are of direct benefit to these persons.
We have heard a great deal recently about the financial difficulties of the farm community and, in particular, about the difficulties which recent figures indicate may be more severe in the prairie regions than in any other region of Canada. A great deal has been said about figures comparing 1970 net incomes in the Prairie region to those in 1969. I think it is important to attempt to put these figures into perspective, Mr. Speaker. Without any doubt, in this region we have gone through a very serious period of difficulty for our farmers. It was a period in which sales were lower than had been expected, a period which, thankfully in this regard, is now past as we approach record sales for this current year. It was a period where their total receipts were bound to be affected by the drop in sales and prices as a whole.
As I say, I think it is important to put the figures in perspective. It has been pointed out that the total net income in the Prairie region has fallen by 36.9 per cent when comparing 1970 to 1969. It is important to note that at the same time net realized income fell by only 1.2 per cent in those two years. That is the real figure on which to pin one's attention when attempting to compare two years like that. The bulk of the additional change, which makes the figure seem so high, results from a change in inventory, a reduction in quantities of wheat which have not been reckoned in terms of the real position in which the farmer is. That inventory had grown larger than he had wanted it, and valuing it at market prices simply distorts the figures. The 1.2 per cent drop is none the less

significant. It is significant particulary because neither of those years might be considered as adequate to provide sufficient income for a very large majority of the producers, and particularly the grain producers in that region.
It is interesting to note that in the figures which led to the conclusion that there was a 1.2 per cent drop in net income between 1969 and 1970, also show a drop on the cost side with regard to operating and depreciation charges as between those two years. While costs generally rise over any period of time, the 1970 figure for operating and depreciation charges is 1.4 per cent lower than it was for 1969. This is no doubt due in part to adjusted farm practices and also to the fact that with the increase in summerfallow and with a decrease in wheat acreage in 1970, lower farm expenses resulted, as had been anticipated.
In that period in 1970, the net realized receipts include, of course, $57 million paid to farmers under the Lift program. The figures for 1969 and 1970 also include a change in the cash advance situation. It is important here to notice that in 1969, the income figure is much higher than it otherwise would have been because in that year farmers relied heavily on cash advances, to the extent that, by the end of 1969, something in the order of $240 million was still owing in cash advances by prairie farmers. That shows as cash receipts for 1969 in those figures. By the end of 1970, the cash advance situation showed an outstanding indebtedness of just over $126 million. This means that in the year a reduction of $115 million in outstanding cash advances had taken place. Hence, the cash position was little changed from one year to the next and, hence again, the net receipt position was little changed from one year to the next.
This adjustment, or this problem of the farmer having to repay his cash advances, was recognized by the government which introduced a number of programs. I mentioned the $57 million which was paid out under the Lift program to farmers. There were, at the same time, significant payments in terms of handling the deficit for the previous wheat, barley and oats pools. A total of approximately $50 million went out in that way. In addition to recognizing those difficulties, the government introduced a number of programs which are now beginning to bear fruit and which will bear fruit in the years ahead.
The program by which the government extends credit facilities to the Canadian Wheat Board is one of the very significant builders for the future. Under this program, in certain cases, the government pays a portion of the interest charge incurred, especially in the case of developing countries which happen also to be developing markets. Some millions of dollars are spent in each year in supporting interest rates connected with wheat sales to these countries. What is not often realized is that for this portion of the program, as for other credit transactions embarked on by the Canadian Wheat Board, if grain is sold abroad on credit the Canadian government guarantees the credit of the buyer. At the present time approxi-
June 30, 1971

mately $300 million in total credit is guaranteed in this way by the government. This means that the total risk of non-payment is shifted from the farmer to the government under this program.
Also as a builder for the future, the government this year introduced the market development program which this year, next year and thereafter, will make available $10 million per year for a variety of imaginative projects for the promotion of our grain sales. Under this program the first expenditure has been allocated to the Canadian grain institute, that being the institute which will be created in Winnipeg, to allow the development there of facilities for demonstrating the best modern methods of milling flour, of crushing rapeseed and handling meal. The program will allow us to bring to Canada from among our customers, people who can learn the advantages there first hand not only of the most modern techniques but also the characteristics of Canadian grain which they may thereafter use in their own countries.
Under this market development head as well, we will be looking at the question of new facilities for product development and for research into new and different ways of moving our product to market. We will also be looking at concrete proposals for the establishment of facilities abroad, where these may assist in the development of markets there. We will be willing to look at proposals for grant, loan or equity assistance where companies in Canada are interested in projects abroad. These may be for the milling of flour, for storage facilities, for crushing facilities for oil seeds or in connection with new ideas which may be brought forward to establish a better place in those markets abroad for Canadian grains.
The Canadian government recognized in total the difficult cash position of the prairie farmer, and this led to the announcement of a package of proposals which were discussed with producers from October until March and which then emerged in legislation. Without these proposals the government, in the fiscal years 1970-71 and 197172, would have been called upon to spend $60 million under TWRA in the first year and $26 million in the second year, for a total of $86 million. It would have been called upon to pay a total of $2 million in connection with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration. The total expenditures without these proposals would therefore have been $88 million.
In the proposals put forward, in place of this $88 million, there is a total program over a two-year period valued at $189.5 million, which is $101.5 million more than would have been spent if there had been no changes. First among these would be the transitional payment of $100 million to prairie farmers. This transitional payment was designed as a result of the recognition of the intention to terminate the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act, effective as of August 1, 1970, and of the fact that benefits under the stabilization program could not begin until the crop year beginning August 1, 1971, had begun. That was to be a transitional payment directly related to the repeal of the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. We recognized the cash needs of the prai-
The Budget-Mr. Lang
rie farmer and desired to put $100 million into the hands of the farmers as quickly as possible.
In addition, under the stabilization program the government would have been committed to expenditures of approximately $36 million in the crop year 1971-72. The prairie farm administration would have continued, at an expenditure of $2 million for those two years. The cost of the administration of the stabilization program would have amounted to about $1.5 million, for a total expenditure of $139.5 million. Also related to these programs was the grassland incentive program which would make available to prairie farmers approximately $15 million in each of 1971 and 1972. In addition, the marketing development program would have put into the cost of the grain selling market $10 million in each year for an overall total of $189.5 million. It is a matter of great regret that the $100 million will now be delayed. This matter was first put forward as a total package and program for discussions with producers in October, 1970. It then went through many months of discussion toward improvements which were announced in March, and was then before this House for many days. Three bills emerged to give effect to this program.
On second reading, these bills were before this House for all or part of 10 days; May 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 14, 17, 20, 26 and 31. One of these, the cash advance changes, seemed to be supported by all who spoke, but none the less members spoke for three days. These bills were in committee on May 18, 20, 25, 26, June 1, 2, 3, 8, 10, 15, 16, 17, 18 and 22. They were back in the House for the report stage, and one was dealt with on June 9, 10 and 22 and again for third reading on June 18 and 21. I refer to the cash advance bill. This amount of House time was spent in an attempt to move these bills forward so that the $100 million could be paid out. It would have been right to pay it out as early as possible because the cash problem of the prairie farmers is particularly serious at the present time.
The record movement of grain which is now taking place, and which gives every sign of continuing, would begin to ease the problem in the year ahead. Cash advances a year ago, June 18, 1970, stood at $190 million. On June 18, 1971, they stood at $71 million. Approximately $119 million have been paid back by farmers who found it less necessary to take advantage of cash advances in that year. This means that the balance owing on cash advances by the end of this crop year will be significantly reduced. This reduction occurred, of course, through the devotion of a significant portion of grain income in the year out of the very rapid movement of grain to the repayment of cash advances.
It was for this reason in particular that it seemed desirable to get this money into the farmers hands as soon as possible. It is now apparent that this will not happen for some months as the legislation has been stalled in the way which I have described. All this time the opposition parties have further taken the position throughout the prairie region of trying to seize upon the

June 30, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Lang
very real difficulties which exist in the farming industry and to distort every attitude and program of the government to cause fear and foreboding as far as possible in the farmers of that region. To some extent, one must agree they have been successful.
It will be important to try and reverse that trend, to emphasize to farmers throughout that region and everywhere that it is the objective of this government to not only help financially, as I have described, but also to do what has to be done whether it be with regard to the quota system or the transportation and handling system to make these parts work well. The individual farmer has no control over these. Therefore, he deserves such support as can be offered to make them work well so that to the greatest extent possible he can obtain from his production the largest possible returns. This does not indicate the over-all level of income the farmer will have. It is not a policy of unlimited support for farmers of any size, but it is a policy of support for all farmers and the emphasis this year is to be in favour of the owner of a small farm, a farm up to a tolerable, effective and efficient size. This is particularly highlighted in the change we propose from the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act to the stabilization plan.
Under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act, the government money went only to wheat. One should ask why wheat and not other grains. This was a bias in favour of one grain and distorted the proper decisions of the individual farmers. It not only went only to wheat, but went on a per bushel basis so that the largest farmers, however large, shared proportionately with the small farmers, however small. It was directly related to the delivery of wheat. If any money came through to the farmer, it came through on a per bushel basis with the largest farmer getting the largest share. If the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act policy of the past is maintained next year, it is estimated that a total of $26 million will have gone into the wheat pool and this is only really maintaining higher stocks in commercial storage than may be necessary. Under the stabilization plan, it is estimated that $36 million will go into the stabilization fund. When this is paid out, it will be paid out within fixed limits so that the very large farmers, those whose gross receipts are over $15,000, do not share in the treasury money which goes into the fund. Whatever money is available is to be divided, particularly among those farmers up to a size of some tolerable efficiency.
It is the determination of this government to use the finances of the treasury to help as much as possible the maximum number of farmers toward a better standard of living and toward an effective operation. The opposition and farm organizations always argue that whatever is paid by the treasury, $200 million or $300 million, more should be paid. They argue this, particularly in the prairie region, while some of their colleagues are apt to be criticizing in other parts of the country every penny that is spent.
In the discussions concerning the stabilization program, no real constructive proposals were put forward with
regard to this policy by farm organizations or the opposition, except the expenditure of more money. They stalled the passage of this legislation and the movement of this very important amount of money into the hands of the farmers because they wanted to emphasize the point that they were all for more money being paid. The truth is, as I indicated when the March 15 motivations of the proposals were announced, that we must always keep under examination the income position of the prairie farmer and what his case for justice is with regard to a better return for his production. I indicated this would be a continuing review. I also indicated that, in the course of the previous fiscal year, we had put into the grain economy from the treasury a total of approximately $300 million as a result of a recognition and understanding of that income position.
In the current year, amounts approaching that order will be expended again, including the $100 million. The immediate cash position led to the conclusion that we should increase treasury payments by $101.5 million through the package of bills I have mentioned, an increase of $101 million in two years. With that, we must still keep the position under review. What does no one any good is the attempt to frighten people about where we are going. Our emphasis on market development, on attempts to improve the total income of prairie farmers through the better selling of their products is one for which I make no apology. I believe this is the right approach. No matter what kind of fiddling with treasury money might be suggested, a far larger proportion of the income of farmers on the prairies will always come from the sale of their products.
It is essential that we continue to pursue all opportunities of market development, that we continue to experience the kind of year we are experiencing now in terms of volume, though hopefully better years in terms of price. Meanwhile, over-all productivity continues to increase. Farmers have done a tremendous job in coping with rising costs by becoming increasingly productive. Particularly in the prairie regions they deserve an immense tribute.

I thank the House for its indulgence. I shall conclude by making only a few additional remarks. The position of the industry must, then, continue to be examined in the light of productivity, in the light of markets which can be obtained and in the light of the improved position in which farmers would find themselves if we could continue to market increasing volumes and allow

June 30, 1971

producers to gain the advantage of applying the technology with which they are familiar.
Hon. members may not realize that in recent years farmers have withheld a great deal of the technology which is known to them; they have not applied fertilizer, for instance, to the extent which would be recommended even in terms of the price of the product, or as would be the case if the marketing of all the product were possible. They have not done so partly because of restrictions due to limited cash and partly because they recognized they would have been producing for storage-and often they knew they were already storing enough from their own economic point of view. This is why we are optimistic that given a concentrated effort to make production as sensitive as possible to market needs we can produce in relation to sales which can be foreseen, and that we can sell ever-increasing quantities.
But whatever we do with regard to improving markets there will always be high sales years and lower sales years and it seems appropriate, therefore, for us to deal with this problem now. What we must avoid, surely, is the spreading of unnecessary fear among farmers. The difficulties they already face in adjusting their operations to changing conditions are already real enough. Changes in technology have meant pressures for bigger farm areas. We must recognize this, and seek to assist those farmers who wish to adapt to their situation. Farmers who wish to acquire additional land should be helped in obtaining it. Our adjustment programs of assistance must also be of help to those who would like to retire from farming. This, again, is part of our current program, a program of expenditure which is likely to be far more productive than putting out money without direct results being achieved.
Much of this effort is made possible through revenues raised in accordance with the budget proposals and through the rearrangement of taxation under our system. I say again that for many farmers in difficulty the improvement in the exemptions will do a tremendous amount year after year to ease the burden they have been carrying as part of the general taxpaying public, and it is therefore a change which I welcome particularly.
