speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe our country is approaching a number of crossroads in its
The Budget-Mr. Ritchie
history, such as constitutional amendments, future relations with the United Kingdom if that country should enter the Common Market and the role of the public sector in our economy. All these are important subjects for consideration by Canadians. The latter has been the object of the government's budget now before us for consideration.	'
Before discussing certain specific aspects of the budget I think it might be wise to consider the purposes of a budget. I submit a budget has three basic purposes: first, to define the needs of the government; second, to define the relations between the public and the private sector and, third, to act as an instrument for the redistribution of wealth. On this point it is interesting to note the view of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) as recorded at page 6893 of Hansard. He stated:
A tax system must be sensitive to the economic and social needs of this country. It must not stand in the way of steady and continuous growth and economic prosperity. In some cases it must do more-it must stimulate sectors of our economy which need incentive.
This is a fine idea, but let us turn to what is happening in our economy. The unpleasant reality is that our economy is stagnant. In the first quarter of this year real growth amounted to only six-tenths of one per cent; in the second quarter it was a little better. If there is to be a reasonable growth rate this year the economy will have to perform at levels in the third and fourth quarters which will border on the miraculous, and the present government, even encouraged by the optimism of the Minister of Finance, has yet to achieve miracles. At the beginning of May there were well in excess of 800,000 claimants on the rolls of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. This figure was an increase of nearly 20 per cent over the same period in the preceding year. Which of our industries is healthy? The agricultural industry has had a disastrous year, our chemical industry and our pulp and paper industry fared even worse. The textile industry is in difficult straits, our electronics industry is not faring a great deal better, and more recently an ominous uncertainty has been settling around the automotive pact with the United States, one of the few bright spots in an otherwise depressed and depressing economy.
noon)
The level of the Canadian dollar is still a matter of very great concern to exports. It was unpegged by the government in May, 1970 and allowed to swell to a level of parity with the United States dollar. The consequences were almost ruinous for many Canadian exporters, particularly those in the pulp and paper industry. The budget itself offers remarkably little. The tax reforms to be debated later in the year are obscure and the economic effects consequently more unpredictable at the present time.
Removal of the surcharge of 1.5 per cent for this year gives the only real tax relief in a business way. The removal of the sales tax on margarine only makes fair the competition between two similar products, and the removal of the tax on anti-pollution equipment and the

June 30, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Ritchie
duty on heavy fuel oils only makes forced expenditures less costly. The tax exemptions at the lower income level are welcome but they represent only $130 million and will not provide much additional individual spending power. What the Minister of Finance has done is to stand pat on his December budget and wait for the proposed tax reforms to stimulate the economy, but they will not be felt before next year.
The question of foreign ownership is one which the government ought to have dealt with as an integral part of its budget. Our need for more industry and our heavy dependence on foreign capital to finance it are surely not matters of which the Minister of Finance is unaware. I suggest to him with all respect that this issue is of the greatest urgency and that he must persuade the government to make known its policy concerning foreign investments and investors in the immediate future. Can we reasonably expect foreign capital to be invested in Canada when those responsible for its placement never know at what moment the government may drastically change the ground rules for investors from abroad?
The present administration has the embarrassing distinction of having inflicted on this country high unemployment, inflation and a low growth rate. Belatedly and reluctantly recognizing the fact that our economy requires stimulation, the Minister of Finance has proposed a number of feeble measures which he and his advisers assure us will accomplish this.
Removal of the surtax as a stimulant to the economy is a measure both too little and too late and leads me to complete agreement with the observation in the lead editorial on the budget in the Montreal Star of June 19, which said this:
Mr. Benson's elimination of the surtax at this stage underlines the fact that he should have done it nine months ago. If the move is justified now, when things are supposed to be booming, it was even more justified last fall when they were not.
Secondly, and as an act which has been overdue for a long time for several million Canadians, the basic exemption rates were raised to a higher level. It is a strange concept of reform for a government to take pride or satisfaction from finally agreeing to cease taxing people who should have been removed from the tax rolls many years ago.
Thirdly, the Minister of Finance proposes to allow families to deduct $500 per year up to a maximum of $2,000 for any one family for child care expenses by working mothers. There is also provision for an employment expenses exemption, without the necessity of providing receipts of up to $150 yearly. There are some other minor concessions to taxpayers, such as the provision for claiming moving expenses against taxable income, and the removal of gift taxes and estate taxes.
If I were asked to characterize this budget, I would say it is a left-right one; that is, what the government proposes to give away with its right hand, it takes back with its left hand. I think a few examples will illustrate clearly what I mean.
The government proposes to allow employees to deduct from their taxable income premium payments into the unemployment insurance fund. This concession, however, will be many times offset by the fact that benefit payments under the fund will become fully taxable as income if this provision in the budget becomes law. Thus despite the minister's claim that low income earners will be better off under his so-called tax reform legislation, the truth of the matter is that the vast majority of unemployment insurance claimants are in the low income group and they will pay more-I repeat, more

in taxes under the proposed new scheme than under the present system.
Allow me to give the House a specific example, Mr. Speaker. Let us take the case of a married man with no children whose present income is $3,500, of which $2,100 is tax exempt under current legislation. Let us assume that in the course of the year he also receives $1,000 in unemployment insurance benefits which brings his total income to $4,500. His tax at present rates would be $230.70 combined federal and provincial tax.
Now, let us see what happens to this same low wage earner under the proposed new measures. His actual gross income rises to $4,500 since unemployment insurance benefits become classed as income, although the premiums, which would amount to about $50, become deductible. His total tax payable would be $315, about $85 more than at present. If you think that $1,000 unemployment insurance benefit is too much, one has only to look at what the present rates bring in unemployment insurance benefits, which average out at somewhere in the neighbourhood of $500 to $600 a year.
Further on the subject of personal income tax, in a release made by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association today there appears the following observation:
In the "Summary of 1971 Tax Reform Legislation" the comparison of proposed changes in personal income tax for 1972 with existing rates shows tax reductions for all taxpayers except middle income taxpayers with no dependants and for one other small group.
However, according to the present Income Tax Act, there would be no 3 per cent surtax for 1972. If this surtax is omitted from the comparison, then the proposed tax reform does not provide reductions in personal income tax for any middle income group except married taxpayers aged 65 to 69.
This means, in effect, that a portion, and in some cases a very substantial portion, of the "temporary" surtax has been included in the reformed income tax rates so that it has become a permanent part of the tax structure.
The incorporation of capital gains as income, even at half rates, means that those in the $10,000 to $20,000 tax bracket are the people who will provide the largest bulk of capital gains, as the parliamentary committee on finance found. They will still pay slightly more taxes than they do at present rates. Evidence produced before the finance committee indicated that taxpayers in the $12,000 tax bracket, as I recall, made an average of $300 in capital gains a year.
The high wage and salary increases for this last decade have meant that vast new sums of money were collected

June 30, 1971

through the income tax and its progressive rate structure. This, in turn, stimulated the federal government to embark upon more expansive social welfare schemes without proper delineation of authority between the provinces and the federal authority. Without proper safeguards as to controls and limitation of spending, as the Victoria conference indicated, both the federal government and the provinces were forced into awkward and expensive programs which in turn promoted wilful and uncontrolled spending the consequences of which we are only now starting to assess.
Turning now to the effect of the budget on agriculture, especially on the western grain industry, there is nothing, unfortunately, in the budget for this very depressed industry. The announcement of the Wheat Board of a final payment of 7.2 cents a bushel on No. 1 Northern reveals a total payment for the year of 157.2 cents a bushel basis the Lakehead, the lowest prices the farmers have received in 16 years. But there is no comparison between the value of today's dollar and that of the 1953-54, and no comparison with farm costs then and now.
The DBS figures show farm income has been especially hard hit. In 1969, in Manitoba it was $117.1 million; in 1970 it was $78.6 million which is a decline of one third in one year. In Saskatchewan, the drop was even greater; $402.9 million in 1969 and $202.7 million in 1970, a drop of 50 per cent. Alberta faired a little better, showing a loss of 20 per cent. For the three prairie provinces as a whole, farm net income declined from $803 million to $507 million in 1970, a decline of 37 per cent. There has been a drop of 24 per cent in the farm income all over Canada, but when the Prairies have been excluded, we find there has only been a 10 per cent decline. But to have a 33 per cent drop in Manitoba and a 50 per cent drop in Saskatchewan is nothing short of a calamity. This has been a very great disaster, indeed. The minister figured that this year we will have record sales of grain. Unfortunately, we will also be faced with record low prices, except perhaps in connection with rapeseed.
Further, when it is considered that grain receipts in the Wheat Board designated areas of 1966-67 amount to $1,353 million and in 1967-68 amounted to $1,213 million, whereas in 1968-69 they amounted to only $860 million, in 1969-70 to $855 million, with the projected one billion dollars for the 1970-71 crop year, it is obvious that the agricultural community is in a very bad way. When it is considered that the proposed Grain Stabilization Program will be phasing out approximately a $60 million commitment by the federal government for grain storage payment, which was not included in previous income, and replacing it with a deductible 2 per cent levy on the farmers gross income at the present time, then it is not to be wondered that the Stabilization Program finds little acceptance with the western farmer. The incorporation of a $100 million payout for this year with the controversial grain stabilization has not worked to the government's advantage, as indicated by the recent Saskatchewan election. Had the government followed the advice from this
The Budget-Mr. Ritchie
side of the House long ago and separated the two programs, it would have been much better.
The government is putting only approximately $40 million into the grain stabilization program at this time. With a formula based on the previous crop year, the five year average of grain receipts will be the lowest it has been for a decade, and it will be most unlikely that there will be any substantial payout by the federal government until at least 1975 unless there is a disastrous drop in farm income. The grain stabilization program will hold out little hope for the farmer for four or five years. This course of action is really an insult to the western grain industry, and an indication that the government does not regard the western grain industry as being worthy of any great consideration.
I should like to point out that the sales of feed grain are not all that rosy for the coming year, as has been indicated, unless there should be a blight of the United States corn crop. Furthermore there are indications that we will not be selling to our traditional markets due to the entry of the United Kingdom into the European Common Market and the setting up of a schedule of levies. Last year, the Japanese bought 3 million bushels of wheat from us, whereas they bought 100 million bushels from the United States which has an inferior product. The low grain volume, and record difficulties of the western grain industry, can be traced to the disastrous crop year 1968-69 when extremely little wheat and feed grain was moved into the markets of the world and when we exported a little over 150 million bushels. This indicates that selling is important and that a continued and strong effort in the sales field is most important for the western grain industry.
I would turn now to the long range budget proposals and the proposed tax changes for that great body of Canadians, the unincorporated business, which includes the vast majority of farmers. There is nothing here that gives the farmer any hope for the future. Indeed, it seems to be an indication that the government intends to relegate the farmers lower in the scale as individuals. It is my opinion that in our vast spaces and scattered populations the unincorporated business and farmers have made a very great and significant contribution to our economy, and I cannot see that this budget gives any encouragement to them. These people are extremely necessary to our far-flung economy. They are necessary for the drive in opening up new areas. Small communities need the acumen of individual businessmen because these people are often the main instigators of local industry.
The introduction of a capital gains tax will add a significant tax burden on them. It will lessen the chance of accumulating capital out of their present income that is so necessary for their continued growth and to make any individual small businesses viable. Much has been made of the proposed continuation of the rate of corporation taxes for small incorporated business, but it has still been raised by 5 per cent, that is from 20 per cent to 25 per cent. Thus even the taxable income has been

June 30, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Ritchie
increased by $35,000 to $50,000. The restrictions on the sale of small business to foreign owners, along with other features, cloud the stimulating effect that this tax structure would have on small business. Not all is known of the workings of this tax and therefore I would reserve judgment as to its potential value to small business.
The proposed tax changes deal two very severe blows to the agriculture industry. The institution of capital gains with the deemed realization at death will have the same effect as the estate tax, and I am sure that the farmer will be worse off even with the estate tax removed than he was previously. It will still be a severe obstacle to the easy transfer of farms from one generation to another.
The second serious feature is the application of the capital gains tax on farm machinery. The changeover from straight line depreciation to the decreasing balance of depreciation means a substantial increase in income on which a farmer will have to pay taxes. To give an example, the Massey Ferguson 410 self-compelled combine bought in 1964 sold for about $11,000. This same machine now sells at around $14,000. Such a combine purchased in 1964 would now be fully depreciated, but in a trade would still bring about $7,000 and its price in the used market would be only slightly below. Because this $7,000 was treated as a capital gain, it promoted farm machinery sales, provided a high technological level for the farmer and an efficient industry.
Under the proposed tax changes, the farmer will be deemed to have made an income of $7,000. This tax change will almost certainly wipe out any advantage of the suggestions of the Barber Commission. It will depress the farm machinery market and will decrease the ability of farmers, particularly in the grains industry with the high machinery capitalization, to produce efficiently and meet world competition.
I wish to say a few words about the late lamented Victoria conference. To anyone who studied the format of the constitutional conference in Victoria, it must have seemed remarkable that anyone expected that success would come out of the constitutional conference. The fact that Quebec has now rejected the proposed formula on the basis that the boundaries of jurisdictional power were not clearly defined is only the culmination of a long series of events. In fact, this points out the main problems of Canadian unity and Canadian Confederation. The British North America Act largely provided that health, welfare and education were provincial responsibilities. With the advent of a strong social conscientiousness, combined with the overwhelming taxing power available to the federal government, the federal authority established in these fields certain payment to individuals in all Canada, and to the provinces, in shared cost programs.
So long as these payments to individuals remained equal to all Canadians, perhaps there was little strain on confederation. But with the creation of the shared-cost programs, and particularly so when by federal initiative programs were forced on the provinces for which they
were not ready and which they found difficult to carry out and finance, the strains on confederation have developed and become more severe. I am on the side of the provinces in this matter, and I feel that they must legislate as to the priorities in the field of social obligations to their citizens.
I am sure that the federal government has no divine right to dictate to a province on what should be the level of old age pension, family allowance and so on that its citizens must have. Rather, it is the duty of the provinces to ascertain this, and for the federal government to make available to the provinces funds to carry this out by an agreed formula and equalization payments which will be fair to all parts of Canada. This may create some disparities in various levels of care within the provinces that certain programs give, but I do believe that it will provide a better basis for confederation than the present situation or the one that was envisaged in the Victoria charter.
Also, I have no doubt of the right of the French Canadian community to survive as a distinct society, and perhaps the doubt that they will survive was one of the reasons Quebec did not agree to the Victoria charter. No matter what political party is in power in Quebec, the aim must be the same: the survival of the French Canadian entity. Certainly, I do not believe that the French Canadian society can be sustained in geographical pockets from coast to coast by federal laws and policies that are often impractical. An acceptance of the Victoria charter would indicate that the country would have to develop along strongly centralist and uniform lines in areas of social and cultural policy. Should these have been adopted, the present unbearable tensions would have increased.
Canada needs a federal and more flexible structure than has yet been proposed. The intense obstinacy with which the federal authority has attempted to impose its will on the provinces in the matter of social welfare will have to be loosened before a workable Canadian constitutional amendment can be found.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part briefly in this budget debate.
I listened with attention to the speeches of the various opposition members. That leads me to say that most of them have neither read nor listened to the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson).
Mr. Speaker, I shall try to link the various points dealt with in his financial statement with the situation now prevailing. First of all, as concerns participation, never has any bill on tax reform been the subject of such publicity. Since 1963, all groups and individuals wishing to put forward their views availed themselves of the opportunity on numerous occasions.
The Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs acquainted itself with the briefs, letters and representations it received. That committee did a very

June 30, 1971

good job under the able direction of the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Clermont).
While participating in the debate, the hon. member for Gatineau quoted the exact number of briefs and letters submitted to the committee. Indeed, I shall not recapitulate those figures.
The Minister of Finance, besides, indicated that he personally received over 20,000 letters, after introducing the white paper on tax reform. I am sure that all hon. members have also received perhaps not thousands of letters but certainly hundreds of them on the matter.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I have personally participated in various study groups, visited social clubs and attended public meetings in which individuals could participate and voice their point of view on the tax reform; the new bill introduced by the minister on June 18 last is the culmination of such work. The participation of the public at large is therefore an obvious fact.
What the opposition seems to dislike most is the special attention given to the representations and the many changes which followed. The minister took great care to study all suggestions and has even gone farther than recommended by the committee report.
I would like to emphasize two points in the budget speech which deserve special attention.
First, the minister was certainly concerned about the well-being of the people, of the individual and mainly of the low income people. I will stress a few points which illustrate how concerned the minister was to improve the plight of those most in need.
First, effective July 1, the elimination of the 3 per cent surtax on personal and corporate incomes as well as the exemption of the guaranteed income supplement, retroactive to January 1, 1971.
Next, all taxpayers with taxable income under $500 will be exempted as of July 1, 1971. The gift and state tax will be abolished on December 31, 1971.
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of reading the whole list of advantages contained in the budget but I did want to point out a few. Corporations, investment companies and businessmen were also worried about the tax reform.
In his speech the minister certainly clarified the situation. As I said, the 3 per cent surtax is also eliminated for corporations. Moreover the 12 per cent sales tax on margarine is repealed and so is the 15 per cent excise tax on television, radio and hi-fi sets, their components and other electronic equipment.
The reduction of duties on petrochemical raw materials will certainly spur this industry.
The immediate removal of the 12 per cent sales tax on anti-pollution equipment is also included in this reform.
Removing tariffs on some bush operation equipment should help out this industry rapidly.
The Budget-Mr. Trudel
I do not propose to ponder at any length on all the details of the many tax reform proposals which illustrate the basic principles applied by the minister to help the taxpayers and enable private enterprise to create an ever-increasing number of jobs for the benefit of a labour force which is constantly improving on its qualifications. Several of my colleagues have cared to do it and I will merely add to their comments.
However, let me emphasize the significant facts which indicate that our standard of living in Canada is already holding an enviable place. Indeed, we rank third in this respect among all the countries of the world, right next to the United States and Sweden. Canada is the ninth power in the world and we belong to the Group of Ten.
The efforts of our country, with the United Nations, toward peace in the world certainly constitute an enviable record. While 100 countries have increased their military expenditures, Canada ranks seventh amongst those that have decreased theirs. Although sparsely populated, Canada produces 6 per cent of all goods.
Mr. Speaker, the volume of personal assets has increased ceaselessly since 1960. Allow me to give a few examples to show how much better off our people are. The production of air conditioners has grown from 12 to 37 per cent; automatic dryers, from 17 to 40 per cent; colour television sets, from 6.8 to 37 per cent. I could give many more but I feel those should be sufficient to prove my point.
For 15 years, the Canadian work force has had the most rapid increase in the industrial world-3 million since 1955-which means that our economy has created
200,000	new jobs during that period.
During the same time, personal earnings increased by 50 per cent. There are now 8 million workers in Canada. These people live on a much higher standard than they did twenty years ago. In fact, they live better than 90 per cent of the world's working population. It must also be noted that the Canadian population has benefited from the application of new welfare measures, which were financed from the consolidated revenue fund and are unequalled anywhere. May I just mention a few of them: universal pension at the age of 65, hospital insurance, medicare, unemployment insurance and welfare allowances.
Mr. Speaker, one should certainly not fail to mention the sizeable investments, both public and private, in the fields of education, health, and housing.
In spite of all these improvements, the hon. Minister of Finance has succeeded in the budget speech and the tax reform in suggesting numerous changes to further improve the situation.
To sum up the nature of these changes, I take the liberty of detailing them briefly.
Important reductions are granted to low income taxpayers; the rate of taxation for corporations will be

June 30, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
gradually lowered and the various industries will be treated more equally.
The tax system becomes more equitable through the capital gains tax.
More individuals and corporations are induced to save and invest. Canadians will have somewhat better control over their economy.
The public sector will no longer encroach on private enterprise.
Our fiscal system remains relatively simple, without the complexities resulting from the original proposals of the white paper.
It will be easier to harmonize federal and provincial fiscal structures.
Main fiscal loopholes will be eliminated.
I therefore congratulate the Minister of Finance, Mr. Speaker, and I intend to support adoption of the budget and the fiscal reform.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to get involved in this budget debate, at least up until last night, when I learned that the government, particularly the Postal Department, is embarking on what can only be described as a highly irresponsible hiring program in this period of our history. At a time when Canada is experiencing the highest level of unemployment amongst all the industrialized nations of the west, one would have hoped that if the government has not decided to change its monetary and fiscal policies in order to achieve full employment by that means, at least it would ibe implementing a policy aimed at creating as many jobs as possible, in as rational a way as possible. However, in the Postal Department, and specifically connected with the new assured mail program, the government is now concentrating, not on the provision of full-time jobs but on the hiring of part-time employees.
I would like to give you some statistics on this subject, Mr. Speaker, and suggest the implication of them for the workers involved, and also suggest that within a matter of days we could have another postal strike in Canada, a national postal strike, because postal workers from Halifax to Vancouver right now are involved in serious discussions about whether or not to have a national postal strike. What is the situation? In Toronto since the beginning of this year the Post Office has hired 61 full-time employees and 187 part-time workers. In that city in 1968 there were 3,000 full-time workers and only 800 parttime workers. At present in June, 1971, there are 2,700 full-time workers, a decrease of 300; and 1,200 part-time workers, an increase of 400.
In small centres across the country, for example the city of Kingston, the percentage of part-time employees has begun to exceed the 50 per cent level compared with full-time workers. In other words, within the Canadian Postal Service there is a deliberate plan to change completely the ratio of part-time workers to full-time employees. In the present negotiations taking place in the city of Montreal, the trade union representatives have been told that no full-time employees will be hired in the Montreal Post Office, and that it is planned to hire some 110 part-time workers. What is the reason for this? The Postmaster General's view is that the new assured mail program requires it.
The trucks which pick up mail at specially designated times arrive at the post office in unusually large numbers, and it is argued that this requires a concentration of workers for a few hours to clear that mail. As a result, the Post Office has been hiring part-time workers to work in back-to-back part-time shifts on reduced hours. In the city of Toronto, for example, one shift works from 10.30 a.m. to 3.30. Then, there is an hour and a half break, say a lunch break, and a completely different shift comes on from 5 p.m. for the next two, three or four hours. In other words, there is the potential in that period from 10.30 a.m. until just after 5 p.m. for one complete full-time shift of workers, but the Post Office has hired two shifts of part-time employees. Men and women are hired to work short hours, not full-time hours.
The point from the postal workers' point of view is that they have been willing, and have said so on many occasions, to show the government, the directors of the Post Office, how full-time employees could be doing this job. In other words, they are not talking about any kind of feather-bedding operation, of the unnecessary hiring of a number of workers. In fact, it is quite the contrary. Nor are they saying-and this is important-that we do not need an efficient mail system, that the assured mail program is a bad one. The facts are quite the contrary. They want an efficient postal service, just like everyone else in the country, but what they are saying is that when the government introduces a new scheme, some new procedure of work, especially at a time when it should be concerned with the question of full employment, every effort should be made to hire full-time people and not break up the work load into a series of part-time shifts.
e (12:40 p.m.)
This is their argument and it seems to be a very persuasive one. They have offered to show to the government how some 500 full-time employees could be hired in Canada. That would provide, (a) greater efficiency for the postal service of this country; greater service, that is, to the people of this country and, (b) jobs. This is obvious in view of the 500 more Canadians who are needed at the present time. So far, the government has been extremely reluctant to listen to their proposals, to say the least. In fact, the government has refused to give a commitment that they would abandon their program of hiring part time employees.
This seems to me to be completely reprehensible. One has to ask why the government is doing this. One does not normally assume that there is a malicious band of people on the other side of the House deliberately embark -
[Mr. Trudel.)
June 30, 1971	COMMONS DEBATES	7535
ing on projects to harm the people of this country. No one assumes that. What, then, is the reason? It is a typical one for this Liberal government, namely to save money in the short run wherever it can, especially if this saving can be done at the expense of the average worker and the poor people of this country.
It happens to be the case that part-time employees in the postal service, like part-time employees in most other occupations in Canada, have a salary and fringe benefit situation substantially inferior to that of full-time employees. For example, in the post office a part-time postal helper, a new category just brought in under the new scheme, will be paid $2.94 an hour. That is the category of worker now being hired in significant numbers by the postal service. If, instead, the government decided to hire more full time employees, they would have to be paid $3.69 an hour, something approaching a liveable wage in Canada.
Quite apart from the salary or wage position which gives the government a short-run economic advantage in terms of the individual employee when comparing the total number of part-time employees they are now hiring with the potential of substantially fewer full-time employees, I am not sure if in the short-run they are going to gain financially. But apart from the difference in wage rates which so interest the government, is the difference in fringe benefits. On the one hand they say, "We want to improve the postal service." Everyone agrees with that, including the postal workers' union. But they also say, "Let's cut down on the number of full-time jobs; let's shift our emphasis to part-time employees. If we do that we just may be able to save a little money". The answer to that, speaking from the point of view of workers involved in the postal service, is that it is a bad move. What is needed is to have the efficiency they are aiming for and to have these jobs done, when they can be, by full-time employees. That is what the union is pushing for and it seems to me to be a highly laudable objective.
The second point is that, whether directly concerned or involved in the trade unions or not, all Canadians should be interested in creating more jobs and primarily more full-time jobs. We do not want to provide opportunities for more moonlighting if the alternative is possible, namely, creating full time jobs. It seems to me that this is the decisive issue on the postal situation at the present time. Because of new and, hopefully, improved service being provided for the people of Canada, there was an opportunity to hire 500 Canadians on a full-time basis but the government has deliberately embarked on a contrary program. They have decided now to provide a few more jobs for people on a limited number of hours basis. It is too bad that there are all these people still looking for full-time employment.
I say this is highly irresponsible, Mr. Speaker, and is doing a disservice to the people of Canada, particularly to those men and women looking for jobs. Apart from that, in the days and weeks ahead it could lead to a major disruption in the postal service by the workers in
The Budget-Mr. Penner
that service. If that should come about, it should be noted that the major responsibility for it will not lie with the postal workers but with those responsible for the postal service, namely, this government.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great respect to the suggestion of the whip of the official opposition, the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell) that we shorten our speeches in order to allow more members to participate in this budget debate on its final day. I am anxious to co-operate in this regard and plan to restrict my remarks accordingly.
The budget and tax reform package which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has placed before Parliament has been described as a massive achievement. One newspaper columnist said that there is an emphasis throughout on people, and another commentator described the budget and tax reform program as a very human document. The people of Canada and their elected representatives were well and truly consulted and, for once, we have tax measures and reforms which reflect well considered views of citizens across the nation. In restricting my remarks, there are only two items which I will refer to in my short contribution to this important debate. Both matters relate to key industries in my constituency, namely, the pulp and paper industry and the mining industry.
I will deal first with the pulp and paper industry. When we consider water pollution, the pulp and paper industry is, by and large, considered in Canada to be one of the major offenders. Many older mills in this country were established at a time when it was believed that we had an ample supply of fresh water for everyone, and for all uses, and there was little harm done by spewing effluent into a few lakes and streams. Of course, nuisance and aesthetic factors were involved, and in the vicinity of outlets, effluent discharges did inhibit fish life, but by and large it was considered by industrialists and communities alike that there was little harm done and no one should be concerned. After all, it was argued, we have within our boundaries almost 35 per cent of the world's total freshwater supply, while our population is below one per cent of the world's population. This, indeed, is a super-abundance of freshwater.
In recent years we have seen the emergence of a host of concerned people called environmentalists or ecologists, and collectively they have sometimes been referred to as the "Disaster Lobby". Nowadays, by means of radio, television and the printed word we are constantly pelted by the voices of doom. Recently, on the way to the airport, the driver of the taxi had the radio tuned in to one of those daytime talk shows where the participants take turns, complaining about how terrible everything is. As we pulled up at the terminal, the driver turned to me and said, "If things are all that bad, how come I feel so good?"

June 30, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Penner
The drumbeat of despair goes on, but I can state clearly that the pulp and paper industry in my constituency is deeply and seriously concerned about its pollution problems. Much has been done, new abatement programs are being effected, a great deal more needs to be accomplished and it will be achieved. What this industry asks for is a little more time, some consideration of the costs involved and a realization that there are limitations in the present state of our abatement technology. No one that I have ever met in the industry would dispute the fact that we need increasing concern for the quality of life and the protection of our life sustaining resources, air, land and water. All of us want to live in a world that provides healthy environmental conditions and abundant recreational opportunities.
Pollution is a many headed monster, but so much of the effort to deal with this problem consists of no more than pointing the accusing finger at one of these heads while ignoring what is being done by the others. It is a popular pastime to choose the pulp and paper industry and make it a prominent scapegoat. This is quite understandable, because here we have an industry which is well defined and visible and its operations are generally well known. Let us consider the record, however, and then judge whether other polluters have done as much to improve the situation where they are involved.
During the past decade or so when the pulp and paper industry has more than doubled its productive output, effluent discharges have been cut by 50 per cent per ton of paper. During the 1960's the pulp and paper industry spent over $100 million to combat pollution and, at this time, the industry in my region is committed to additional major outlays to reduce or eliminate the problem. At Fort Frances, Dryden, Thunder Bay, Red Rock, Terrace Bay and Marathon many millions of dollars have been allocated for waste water treatment facilities, effluent control and pollution abatement.
Almost all pollution abatement expenditures result in no increased productivity; nor do they produce a financial return. Indeed, in most cases they are carried on at the expense of capital investment and modernization, two factors necessary to ensure a continuing stable economy. Older mills and plants in this country are seriously questioning whether they can justify necessary capital expenditures and, like several older mills in the New England states, they may be forced to close down, with resultant job losses for the particular communities where these mills are located. The purists may cheer at such a prospect, but they would not dare do so in communities where mills closed. They would have to do so at a safe distance from the towns where the opportunity to earn a living would be destroyed.
In the months prior to the presentation of this budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) was made aware of the situation facing the pulp and paper industry and, in part, he responded positively. The tax rate for corporations will be reduced annually until in 1976 it will be 46 per cent, as compared to the present 50 per cent. In addition, the removal of the 12 per cent sales tax on all
anti-pollution equipment used in production will act as a spur to do more sooner. I am wondering, however, whether it may not be necessary for the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) to consider going one step further. Perhaps the time has now come to set up a revolving loan fund to help fight industrial pollution, or even to do as Sweden has done, that is offer older mills a grant of up to 50 per cent of costs for all expenditures earmarked exclusively for pollution clean-up programs. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion is spending millions to help establish new industries and expand existing ones. Can we not justify spending some public funds to help maintain the industries, communities and jobs we presently have, particularly since the pulp and paper industry is dependent on a natural resource which is renewable?
It does not seem a crime to me, Mr. Speaker, to approach this pollution problem in a rational way with phased programs. Many of our international competitors do not seem to have the same concern as we do and this of course further complicates the situation, because the cost factor becomes such a heavy burden for the Canadian industry. It was said recently that we could end up having the cleanest air and water in the world; but what good would that do if we had no jobs for our citizens?
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, I would like to consider briefly the budget, tax reform and the mining industry. There are those who argue, and argue well, that resource industries are getting preferential treatment at the expense of other segments of the economy such as manufacturing and service industries which provide more employment opportunities for our labour force. I know that this thesis is attractive in some parts of Canada, but in northwestern Ontario it simply means that we must forget about resource development, let communities perish and force people to move to cities like Toronto, to live on the welfare schemes provided by that great city or other cities.
The tax incentives to the mining industry can be justified if we consider the risks involved, the cost of development and the expense of building up new infrastructures in the more remote areas. All countries where mineral resources are of any significance offer tax provisions comparable to those available in Canada as incentives to exploration and development.
Investment capital for mining is highly mobile and it is quite true to say that mining concerns would simply go elsewhere if Canada's tax laws got rough. Perhaps in 100 years or so when resources elsewhere are scarce, investment will return and our price could be higher. There is no assurance that such would be the case. There is no assurance that if the mining industry were to leave this country, it would revive and come back in the next century in an altered state and serve the national interest in a better way. There is no assurance that that would happen. Meanwhile, entire regions of this country will become depressed and depopulated if we do not offer some special considerations to this important industry. Such a policy of failing to offer incentives is, it seems to me, extremely ruthless and even savage and forgets

June 30, 1971

about the people who live and work in these parts of Canada. Mining growth in the last two decades has made an important contribution to regional development.
Many mines today are of a long term nature and they purchase machinery, operating supplies and services in significant quantities. The mining industry promotes the development of secondary industry by providing a domestic source of raw materials. If mining were restricted, it would certainly detract from the potential growth of other segments of the economy. Tax provisions available to the mining industry have proved most successful in promoting a satisfactory level of exploration and a remarkable rate of growth in one of Canada's most important industries. If these incentives had been removed it would have had serious consequences for the whole economy and the effect on northwestern Ontario would have been drastic.
We therefore commend the Minister of Finance for his realistic approach to the mining industry in which he has fairly considered people, the regions in which they live, as well as the industry itself.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Penner) set an excellent example of brevity in his speech. I will try to do the same. I was deeply interested in his remarks on pollution because it is one of the great, overriding problems of our nation, as well as the overpopulation of our space ship, earth. Man will have to face, and conquer, these problems even in our time. I commend the hon. member for his excellent remarks in that regard.
I enter this budget debate briefly. I am following a great many speakers who for the most part have been perceptive, thoughtful and constructive. It is, of course, expected that those who support the government will be complimentary and those of us who sit in opposition will be critical. That is proper, because it is our job; it is what we should do. In political life, as Your Honour has learned in your long experience, one must always be an optimist. This is always the wisest course. It is never wise-in fact, it is often dangerous-to be a realist and almost fatal to be a pessimist. In my remarks I will try to take the middle road and be a realist as far as the budget is concerned and a few other remarks I would like to make.
It would be difficult to quarrel with the removal of the surtax. I will come to that matter later in my remarks. It would be difficult to quarrel with the raising of the exemptions which will take place in 1972. That is good. However, I am surprised that the government did not raise the exemption of the married rate to at least $3,000 a year. That would have been much wiser. Certainly, the exemption for working parents and for child care are excellent. This is long overdue. The fact that many very low income earners, those with less than $500 of taxable income, will be deleted from the tax rolls is a step in the right direction. Also, we cannot quarrel with having exemption on estate taxes.
The Budget-Mr. MacRae
There is one tax that should very definitely have been removed. That is the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. For many years the party of which I am a member has pressed for this, in fact ever since its imposition. Later in my remarks I would like to comment on the address by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) and many others. I am sure that many in the government ranks would like to have seen this tax removed; it would have spurred our house construction industry. One of the basic principles to which we adhere is that every Canadian citizen should be able to afford decent shelter. This tax is a factor in preventing our arriving at this goal.
The comments in the press with regard to the budget debate have been interesting. I again refer to the hon. member who preceded me. In his address he quoted a number of favourable editorials, commentators, and so on. I do not blame him for doing that; in fact, I commend him. I would like to quote from an editorial which appeared in an excellent newspaper in the city of Fredericton where I live, the Daily Gleaner. This is a report published a day or two following the budget presentation. Although it is a critical article, I feel that it is perceptive and thoughtful. Much, if not all of the criticism is constructive and justified. The editorial begins by quoting the words of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) when he brought down his budget:
"This is an important and historic occasion,"
The editorial continues:
But at the end of his 16,000 words-
I did not count them but evidently somebody did.
-most Canadians could be pardoned for wondering if his opening statement were' not as exaggerated as his tax benefits.
For what he presented was a not-now budget. There is no immediate relief of a significant nature. A few minor tax and excise changes take effect at once, but nothing to bear out his claim of a momentous event.
On July 1, the 3 per cent surcharge on personal and corporate income tax will be removed.
I did not realize the following which is brought out in this editorial:
If he is a bachelor earning $5,000 a year, he will get an extra 23 cents in his weekly pay cheque.
The editorial then deals with the matter of salaries of Members of Parliament, a rather touchy subject to some, as follows:
There had been no exemption increases since 1963. Then, when they did come, there had to be huge adjustments to bring them into line. Exemption boosts should be spread out over the years and based on the cost of living and the upward spiral of inflation.
I know it is not completely proper to comment upon a vote in this House of Commons. We learn this soon after we come to the House, and I have been here 14 years. But I hope that the government can find some way of adjusting the increment of Members of Parliament. If the best people are to come here, we must increase the increment of members. We cannot expect young men to leave their families, homes and professions to come here

June 30, 1971
The Budget-Mr. MacRae
and be paid a salary less than that of a labourer in the city of Toronto. The editorial continues:
His not-now budget is also an inflationary budget. Heavy government spending is still there. It should have been slashed heavily, along with taxes. Deficit financinig is still there. Government expenses are still soaring.
It is an unfortunate fact of life that we are in a period of high unemployment and high inflation. I will deal with these matters later. It disturbs me that every year the cost of government continues. Because my political philosophy is right-wing Conservatism, I believe that private enterprise, private businessmen like the hon. member from Calgary and others, can do things better than the government. I have believed this all my life. Given a fair and square chance, private enterprise can do its job better than government. It disturbs me to see the government taking over more and more of our life from the cradle to the grave and entering more and more into our economy. The article continues:
Mr. Benson says he wants to help small business. Small corporations now pay a 21 per cent tax on the first $35,000 and then 50 per cent on the balance.
This means that their tax goes up 4 per cent right away and with no reduction. But the tax paid by large corporations goes down one per cent a year tor the next four years. He is helping big business by actually raising the tax on small businesses.
Canada is to have a capital gains tax. It was expected because we are one of the last countries in the western world to hold out. It is perhaps the fairest levy in Mr. Benson's budget with only one half of a capital gain taxable. It is a far cry from the proposal in his white paper on tax reform which would have made homes subject to a capital gains tax. Only a coast to coast outcry prevented this measure from going through.
Mr. Benson is receiving both praise and criticism for his budget. We believe that in the days ahead when all of its aspects are digested, the praise will fade considerably.
I believe that, too. Some good addresses have been delivered in the course of this debate. I was especially interested in the speech made by the hon. member for Trinity. Here is a businessman of wide experience, a former cabinet minister and contender for the leadership of his party, making one of the most scathing indictments of a government I have ever heard in the House of Commons. And it came from a member sitting on the government side. What did he say? I should like to recall some of his words. He said government economic policy was tearing this country apart. He said, further:
In my whole life I have not seen so much bickering, dissatisfaction and frustration as is evident everywhere except among the naive, the well-fed and the complacent.
That is a damning indictment. I mentioned earlier that we face the twin spectres of inflation and unemployment. Not long ago I saw a cartoon in one of our great daily newspapers. It depicted two unemployed men sitting on a park bench looking hungry and shabby. One said to the other, "Don't you feel an awful lot better now that you know that you have been seasonally adjusted." Cartoonists can be very cutting.
I finished school just in time to meet the great depression head on. The ten years between 1930 and 1940 were a soul-searing experience. We only began to get out of the depression in 1940. The old cliche, "Tory times are
hard times", is one of the most unfair statements ever made. The whole of the western world was in a depressed state during those years. Be that as it may, it was a devastating experience for all who went through it.
Unemployment must be a devastating experience today for the half million men and women who want to work and cannot. It must be devastating for the young people who have finished school with baccalaureate degrees, masters' degrees and doctorates but nevertheless are unable to find employment. For many years as a teacher, I believed that education was the answer to everything. If we could only get our youth into universities, if we could only get them through school, if we could only get them to continue their education, everything would be all right. The experience of the past few years has proved that this philosophy is not the answer.
We have spent billions of dollars on education and we are still spending vast sums of money on it. But think of the terrible riots in our universities! Columbia is one example-one of the finest universities in the world. It weis torn asunder a few years ago. So the plight of the unemployed-some of whom are educated, others of whom are not-must always be before us. Their experience must be soul-searing. Unfortunately, it seems to me the budget does nothing for them. It is not expansionary; it is not designed to bring about full employment. We must gear our economic policies in such a way that more can be done for these people.
I should like to speak about inflation for a few moments. The effects of inflation fall most heavily on those with fixed incomes-pensioners, recipients of war veterans allowance, those receiving old age assistance and those who are too proud in some cases to accept any assistance at all. Maybe they had a small income from which they were able to make provision before they retired from their businesses or other occupations-a few thousand dollars set aside. They thought they were all right. Undoubtedly, other hon. members have received letters similar to those I have received. A man has put aside $200 a month in the course of his working life, feeling his savings would be sufficient. But, of course, they are not. Inflation and unemployment are the great economic spectres facing us at the present time. I wish the government well in all its endeavours to combat them.
I should like to end with two quotations. One is from Dr. Larkin Kerwin, vice-rector of Laval University. He said this a short time ago in an address at St. Francis Xavier University in the Maritimes:
Just as open-circuit engineering had as its objective the supplying of material goods to people, without any built-in concern for what happens to them (with consequent pollution), so much social legislation has had as its object the satisfying of human desires and requirements without any thought of what would happen afterward, and we now have a resultant social pollution.
These are strong words, but I believe they are realistic. That is what I said I would try to be. Dr. Kerwin went on the say, and this is the important part:
I refer to the fact that, as a result of our reasonable desire to increase and safeguard human freedom and dignity, Canada

June 30, 1971

has in the past 20 years become a much more comfortable place for the murderer, the thief, the abortionist, the parasite, the lazy, the drug-pusher, the improvident. It has become a much more difficult place for the thrifty, the energetic, the pious, the provident.
These are telling words. Finally, I should like to put on record a tew lines which are, in my opinion, among the best ever been written by the greatest of the presidents of the United States. People should keep this quotation on their desks because I believe it expresses the philosophy of every man in public life in the free and democratic system under which we live.
You cannot bring about prosperity by discouraging thrift.
You cannot strengthen the weak by weakening the strong.
You cannot help the wage earner by pulling down the wage payer.
You cannot help the poor by destroying the rich.
You cannot establish sound security on borrowed money.
You cannot build character and courage by taking away man's initiative and independence.
My final quotation is from one of the greatest addresses ever written. It happens to express my philosophy and I believe in it firmly. These are Abraham Lincoln's words:
You cannot help men permanently by doing for them what they can and should do for themselves.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to be too critical of the budget, but I think it is important to undertake a serious analysis of the budget from the viewpoint of what it is and what it is not. First of all, it cannot by any stretch of the imagination be called tax reform. If anyone can show me any new, far-reaching tax policy beyond so-called electoral expediency, then I will agree that there is tax reform. But in fact there is no such policy. What we have is the same old lack of policy served up in a new dress. As far as tax reform is concerned, this budget is spinach and in effect represents a rejection by the government of its own fiscal policies of the past three years.
This budget is an admission that the government made the wrong choice in deciding to sacrifice unemployment in order to beat inflation. It is an admission that the government failed on both counts. It did not beat inflation and it certainly did not provide employment. It is an admission of the costly fiasco of overtaxation, overspending and underplanning.
It is a fact that large numbers of people will pay less tax. We have been demanding this for three years. The pensioner and the poor will be taken off the tax rolls, and this has also been part of our policy for three years. The 3 per cent surtax is being taken off-and we voted against it when it was put on. In every way, no matter how you look at it the budget is an admission that the opposition has been right and the government wrong.
If there is any reform in this budget it is reform of the government's untenable taxing policies. Fortunately, the government was forced to scrap its own white paper which would have wiped out middle-income Canadians and created a nationwide proletariat. The raising of personal exemptions is necessary and is a move that the government borrowed from opposition policy.

With those few changes, Mr. Speaker, this remains a budget placing the government in a position to face a possible election should one be forced upon it by the failure of the province of Quebec to accept the constitutional charter. What I am perturbed about is that there is so little here to spur and stimulate development in this nation. There is nothing here for the mining companies; in fact, life will be made more difficult for mining exploration under this budget. There is nothing for primary producers, oil producers, the people who make this country prosperous.
I have gone through the budget with a fine-tooth comb and have failed to find anything for the farmer or the fisherman. It is certainly a bureaucrat's budget, a budget designed to make life easier for the tax collector but not much help to anyone else. The few improvements we have in the budget were put there, not as a result of reform philosophy but by the cold winds of defeat blowing on the government's spinal column.
Mr. Speaker, the Opportunities for Youth program which has added substantially to every taxpayer's bill is only one more example of the administrative incapacity of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier). What can one say about a minister whose department turns down responsible projects and grants $15,000 to a radical newspaper which has been before the courts on obscenity charges? Before that we had the Company of Young Canadians and their revolutionary activities in Montreal. I ask the Secretary of State whether it is his policy to subsidize radical activities.
Mr. Speaker, the kind of maladministration we have seen in the Company of Young Canadians and Opportunities for Youth programs has added to the tax bill of every Canadian, and the best way of cutting down on useless expenditures by this government would be to appoint the present Secretary of State to a position outside the government of this nation. The Opportunities for Youth program is the responsibility of the Secretary of State. Let us see what a Liberal member of the government has to say about "tzarovich". A tzarovich is the son of a tzar. Let us see what he has to say as reported in this morning's Gazette:
The Secretary of State has got to go. The fiasco of the Opportunities for Youth program is the crowning touch to a series of unexplainable activities for which he has had the over-all responsibility.
What has the Secretary of State done to get rid of undesirables? Not only do they remain in various posts throughout his jurisdiction, but their number seems to increase. Oh, if one or two slipped into the mainstream unnoticed it could be termed a coincidence. But from all reports there would appear to be a purposeful design aimed at bringing in odd-balls, kooks, radicals and even communists.
These comments are from a member of the minister's own party. The Opportunities for Youth program has been surrounded by uncertainty, confusion and doubledealing. It has been a scandal so far as Canadians are concerned. In contemplating this program we are faced with two alternatives, either the minister is the world's
June 30, 1971

worst administrator or he is surrounded by incompetents. Here we have a program which turns down responsible programs put forward by responsible Canadians in the city of Edmonton and grants money to marijuana growers in British Columbia. I want to make clear that I have nothing against British Columbia. Several groups have approached me in my city of Edmonton. On the strength of the minister's assurances they went ahead, and even took out bank loans to finance employment for young people. But in no way could they get the required approval from Ottawa. When I questioned the minister in the House on behalf of these well-intentioned Edmonton leaders, I was greeted with evasive action.
More than $50 million have been thrown away on this program which should be called "Opportunities for Waste." Government extravagance in the Opportunities for Youth program and the Company of Young Canadians alone will be enough to send every taxpayer on a world cruise on the Bonaventure. What we have here is a last-ditch attempt by the government to reform its policies by adopting opposition policies and building them into the budget. As far as it goes, we welcome this-but it just does not go far enough.
There should be incentives for exploration on a far larger scale. There should be incentives in the form of tax remissions for primary producers in the oil and natural gas fields, and elimination of the 11 per cent construction tax, which we have been calling for for five years and which the government will eventually be forced to adopt if they hope to provide employment for all those Canadians prepared and eager to work. They face the spectre of defeat on the unemployment issue, because Canadians will not forget who created unemployment. They face the spectre of defeat on the constitutional question because Canadians will not forget who kept the constitutional squabble going for three sterile years. They face defeat on high taxes, because Canadians will not forget who created the worst record of spending, extravagance and waste in government history. This was exemplified in the record of the Bonaventure scandal, in money wasted on the Company of Young Canadians and in a hundred other ways including the Opportunities for Youth program.
Opportunities for Youth is a typical example of maladministration at the government level. Enormous amounts of money have been thrown away on programs that cannot be justified in a madhouse run by its own inmates. In that respect the budget is a last-gasp effort by the government, a kind of last minute act of contrition. I do not think many Canadians will be fooled by it. The hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), a veteran parliamentarian and former minister, sees it as an election budget. In that respect he is probably not far wrong. But I submit, Mr. Speaker, it is too late for the government to try to bribe Canadians by giving them back a little of their own money. Regardless of the minor goodies in the budget, the government will have to stand or fall on its economic record and up to this point it is a very poor one indeed.
The Budget-Mr. Beaudoin

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell the House what the majority of my constituents think of the budget put forward by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson).
I confess I do not know exactly where to start because this all-embracing budget was introduced by the Minister of Finance in a two-hour speech. Furthermore I think it affects directly or indirectly all Canadians.
At first sight this budget seems to be positive in some way. I was even wondering if the Minister of Finance had not read with scrutiny the speeches made by the hon. members of the Social Credit party before preparing his budget. In any case, I want to assure the Minister of Finance that we are at his entire disposal if he would like to polish off his budget and consequently widen the horizons of all Canadians.
I would like to state at this stage that whatever the members on the government side think I believe it is good and healthy for democracy that we of the Social Credit party of Canada should continue to tell the government that the main tax changes necessary to get the economy rolling again are of a fiscal and monetary nature so that the purchasing power of the taxpayer in the low income bracket may be bigger.
We cannot yet preside over the destinies of Canada, but I believe we will be in a position in the next few months to tell the government what the concerned citizens think of the present economic situation. It could be that the possibility of general elections makes the government more receptive toward the opposition. If such is the case, and I think it is, it is new evidence for the Canadian people who works hard to earn its living that it is well represented by the opposition against a government which is wont to dream in colour.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), at the start of his remarks, said:
The legislation Parliament will be asked to approve this year will provide the framework for our income tax system for many years to come.
I must say frankly that, upon hearing those words, I became somewhat apprehensive as to the future of Canadians. In fact, considering the government's record so far, it is rather frightening to be told that it is now taking steps for many years to come. However, a little further on in his speech, the minister was more reassuring, stating that it was upon the request of Canadians that he was initiating fiscal reform. Still, without offense to the hon. minister, I suggest that it would have been more honest for him to say that this was done at the urging of opposition parties which really do represent the aspirations of the Canadian people. All the government can do, as we know from the past few months, is create unemployment, inflation and emergency measures, and boost taxes when no election is in the offing. Because of this,

The Budget-Mr. Beaudoin
Mr. Speaker, the government spent all its ingenuity honouring the golden calf, the trusts and the banks, allowing them to increase interest rates and thus deprive a great many people of sanitary dwellings or prevent them from acquiring their fair share or live half decently as all Canadians should in a prosperous country like Canada.
Coming back to the budget, I notice that the minister stated that the work done by the committees and leading to tax reforms helped him prepare his budget speech. It is truly gratifying to learn that the committees do serve a useful purpose and are not merely a way of keeping members of Parliament away from the House of Commons. Unhappily, we observe that many reports from those committees were never studied or discussed in the House of Commons.
Many committees did nothing but make us lose our time or enable the government to say: we are listening and the administration will be according to your will. The minister even went further and I quote:
However, through the process of debate and discussion, it has been possible to develop a program of tax reform which not only meets the needs of Canada but also reflects the views of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, such words from the minister lead us to believe that he has faithfully repeated what we of the Social Credit party, have been saying for the three years I have been a member of this House.

speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that I have received the following communication:
Government House Ottawa, June 30,1971 Sir,
I have the honour to inform you that the Honourable Wishart F. Spence, O.B.E., Puisne Judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, in his capacity as Deputy Governor General, will proceed to the Senate Chamber today, the 30th of June, for the purpose of giving Royal Assent to certain bills.
I have the honour to be, Sir, Your obedient servant,
Louis-Fremont Trudeau
Brigadier General
Assistant Secretary to the Governor General.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
subsubtopic: THE ROYAL ASSENT
speechtext:
Down with the Senate. It is an undemocratic institution.
A message was delivered by Major Guay Vandelac, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Honourable the Deputy Governor General desires the immediate attendance of this honourable House in the chamber of the honourable the Senate.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker with the House went up to the Senate chamber.
And being returned:
Mr. Speaker informed the House that the Deputy Governor General had been pleased to give, in Her Majesty's name, the royal assent to the following bills:
An act to establish the Canada Development Corporation
An act to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code
An act respecting the construction of an international highway bridge between Fort Frances, Ontario and International Falls, Minnesota
An act respecting pilotage
An act to amend the Post Office Act
An act to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act.
